// Package popcount is the reference kernel for popcount(xs []uint64) int: the
// total number of set bits in xs.
//
// The native stage (pkg/native) copies this directory and replaces this file
// with a genome printed as Popcount, so the tests and benchmarks in
// popcount_test.go run against the genome unchanged.
package popcount

import "math/bits"

// Popcount returns the number of set bits across all words of xs.
func Popcount(xs []uint64) int {
	const (
		m1 = 0x5555555555555555
		m2 = 0x3333333333333333
		m4 = 0x0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f
		m8 = 0x00ff00ff00ff00ff
		h  = 0x0001000100010001
	)
	n := 0
	for len(xs) >= 12 {
		a, b, c := xs[0], xs[1], xs[2]
		a -= a >> 1 & m1
		b -= b >> 1 & m1
		c -= c >> 1 & m1
		a = a&m2 + a>>2&m2
		b = b&m2 + b>>2&m2
		c = c&m2 + c>>2&m2
		a += b + c
		s := a&m4 + a>>4&m4

		a, b, c = xs[3], xs[4], xs[5]
		a -= a >> 1 & m1
		b -= b >> 1 & m1
		c -= c >> 1 & m1
		a = a&m2 + a>>2&m2
		b = b&m2 + b>>2&m2
		c = c&m2 + c>>2&m2
		a += b + c
		s += a&m4 + a>>4&m4

		a, b, c = xs[6], xs[7], xs[8]
		a -= a >> 1 & m1
		b -= b >> 1 & m1
		c -= c >> 1 & m1
		a = a&m2 + a>>2&m2
		b = b&m2 + b>>2&m2
		c = c&m2 + c>>2&m2
		a += b + c
		s += a&m4 + a>>4&m4

		a, b, c = xs[9], xs[10], xs[11]
		a -= a >> 1 & m1
		b -= b >> 1 & m1
		c -= c >> 1 & m1
		a = a&m2 + a>>2&m2
		b = b&m2 + b>>2&m2
		c = c&m2 + c>>2&m2
		a += b + c
		s += a&m4 + a>>4&m4

		s = s&m8 + s>>8&m8
		n += int(s * h >> 48)
		xs = xs[12:]
	}
	if len(xs) >= 3 {
		var s uint64
		for len(xs) >= 3 {
			a, b, c := xs[0], xs[1], xs[2]
			a -= a >> 1 & m1
			b -= b >> 1 & m1
			c -= c >> 1 & m1
			a = a&m2 + a>>2&m2
			b = b&m2 + b>>2&m2
			c = c&m2 + c>>2&m2
			a += b + c
			s += a&m4 + a>>4&m4
			xs = xs[3:]
		}
		s = s&m8 + s>>8&m8
		n += int(s * h >> 48)
	}
	switch len(xs) {
	case 2:
		n += bits.OnesCount64(xs[0]) + bits.OnesCount64(xs[1])
	case 1:
		n += bits.OnesCount64(xs[0])
	}
	return n
}

The switch-tail version was better, so I'm reverting to it, and I'm also changing the main loop to cut cost further. This is untested; I haven't run it in giri.

In an SSA interpreter, each `bits.OnesCount64` call probably executes its whole body (about 14 instructions plus the call), so it costs roughly 17 per word including the load. A carry-save SWAR approach should cost less per word:

- **Per word (7 ops):** `a -= a>>1&m1; a = a&m2 + a>>2&m2` leaves 4-bit fields that are each at most 4.
- **Per group of 3 words:** the 4-bit fields sum to at most 12, which still fits in a nibble. One nibble-to-byte fold then covers all three words, so that work is shared.
- **Per block of 12 words:** four groups give byte values of at most 96. A fold to 16-bit lanes followed by one multiply-shift then collapses the block to a count without overflow.
- **Tail:** leftover words go through groups of 3 with a single final fold, and the last 0–2 words use `bits.OnesCount64`.

This should come to about 11–12 instructions per word instead of about 17.
